 The only point which requires consideration in this appeal is whether the tenancy created in favour of the defendant by Jatindra Nath Bose in the year 1936 is a protected interest under section160(g), Bengal Tenancy Act. This section was enacted to protect a right created with the express permission in writing of the landlord at whose instance the tenure or holding was sold. In order that a lease granted by a defaulting tenant may be a protected interest under this clause, the power to grant it must have been given "expressly and in writing" by his lessor. We have accordingly to consider whether Jatindra Nath Bose was "expressly and in writing" given the power to grant the lease of the description which has been granted in favour of the defendant.  "There can be no denying the fact that the plaintiffs sought to challenge the acquisition of their Hats and Bazars made under the general notification dated 2-4-56 issued under section 3(1) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and so it is directly hit by President's Order No.  90 of 1972, which gives a clear mandate of law that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits , appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No.  XXVIII of 1951) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1956 (EB Ordinance No.  III of 1956) or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders passed in such suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceeding shall cease to have any effect: and no Court shall entertain and no person shall bring any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question. 

 38. We had occasion, in Civil Appeal No.  46 of 1979. People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigraha wherein the acquisition of debtors estate by general notification dated 2-4-56 under section 3(1) of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was challenged, to hold on a reference to President's Order No.  90 of 1972, that the directive in law is clear, that, on coming into operation of this Order, notwithstanding earlier view of the law on the subject, a pending proceeding seeking to challenge or call in question the acquisition of any property under any of the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall abate and no proceedings shall be in stated in any Court. 

 40. From a mere reading of the provisions of the two President's Orders quoted earlier it is clear that President's Order No.  69 of 1972 envisages abatement of all kinds of suits or other legal proceedings against the Government of Bangladesh whether or not related to acquisition under the Act when the Government opts not to be a party thereto, while President's Order No.  90 of 1972 seeks abatement only of suits and other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No.  XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (EB Ordinance No.  III of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question. President's Order No.  69 of 1972 covers a much bigger field than President's Order No.  90 of 1972. President's Order No.  69 of 1972 is so to say the genus of which President's Order No.  90 of 1972 is specie. Article 2 of President's Order No.  90 of 1972 begins with the phrase "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". Such a non-obstante clause, it is true, has the effect of abrogating the provisions of prior statute in the event of a conflict between the same and the new statute. But such a non-obstante clause cannot reasonably be read as overriding anything contained in any relevant existing law which is not inconsistent with the new statute. We are unable to see any inconsistency or mutual exclusiveness between the two President's Orders both of which aim at abatement of a suit. As logical sequel the provisions of President's Order No.  69 of 1972 cannot be said to have been abrogated because of the non-obstante clause added to President's Order No.  90 of 1972. 

 41. One might notice that, although redundant, the Government of Bangladesh made an application for abatement of the suit even under President's Order No.  90 of 1972. Therefore, we have to look into the facts disclosed in the plaint and the prayers made there in to see whether the plaint was hit by the President's Order No.  90 of 1972. The learned Judge of the High Court Division opined that paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint and prayer No.  (ii) thereof came within the mischief of President's Order No.  90 of 1972 and not the rest of the allegations and the prayer. We think that not only the allegations in paragraph 14-16 and prayer No. (ii) had abated but also the suit itself had abated as a whole, being hit by Article 2 of President's Order No.  90 of 1972. The averments in the plaint and the prayers made therein amount to a challenge of the acquisition of the wakf estates concerned, apart from a challenge of EB Ordinance No.  III of 1956 as noticed by the learned Judge of the High Court Division. In the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigraho, 33 DLR (AD) 13 this Court had the occasion to consider the question of abatement of a suit under President's Order No.  90 of 1972 in a similar case. The prayers in the case were couched in more or less identical terms as in the present case. The plaint of that suit was found to have been hit by President's Order No.  90 of 1972."

Another fact that requires to be noted is that President's Order No. 90 of 1972, the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (Third) Order 1972, was promulgated on 3rd August, 1972 long after the observation made in some of the decisions of the High Court, Dacca on the retention by the Mutwalli or Shebait of an estate on account of non-preparation of the compensation assessment roll. This enactment made in President' Order No.  90 of 1972 clearly states that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No.  XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1956 (EB Ordinance No III of 1956) or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all order, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders passed in such suit, appeals applications and other legal Proceeding shall cease to have any effect; and no court shall entertain and no person shall bring fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question."
